newsitem.title: HUNGARY: NATO joiners to cooperate after Madrid - Hungary.
newsitem.headline: NATO joiners to cooperate after Madrid - Hungary.

text.p: East European countries hoping to join NATO will coordinate policies after a Madrid summit on expansion but not before, Hungarian Foreign Minister Laszlo Kovacs said on Monday.

"What we agreed is that after the Madrid decision if everything goes well and those countries will be invited to start talks on accession then we will harmonise our policy vis a vis NATO," Kovacs said after talks in Budapest with visiting Czech Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec.

"And of course we are going to harmonise our policy with all the other countries of the first wave of enlargement like Poland and maybe one or two more countries," Kovacs told Reuters after a news conference.
Asked if the aspiring new members were coordinating policy beforehand, Kovacs said, "It wouldn't be right."
"The position of Poland is exactly the same," he added.

"Poland is closely cooperating with Czech Republic and also with Hungary and we are in full agreement with our Polish colleagues that when the decision is made in Madrid then the three four or five (chosen) should closely cooperate when approaching NATO..."
Hungary, Poland and Czech Republic are considered the front runners for NATO expansion, with Slovenia and Romania also deemed strong contenders.
Zieleniec and Kovacs said the recent agreement between NATO and Russia aimed at defusing Moscow's concerns about enlarging the Western military alliance had boosted prospects for their membership.

"After the Madrid summit it will be obvious which countries will start negotiations with NATO and after that countries that will be in the first round should have close and intensive relationships (among themselves)," Zieleniec said.
"That is the moment when these countries should think about exerting their influence on the NATO-Russia negotiations," he added.
Kovacs said Eastern Europe in general hailed the agreement between NATO and Russia.
"We are satisfied that this agreement is not a setback for the countries that would like to join," he said.

"There is no second class membership and all the countries that join should get the same rights," he added, referring to concerns before the agreement that Russia would demand that new members not have the same rights and responsibilities as other NATO members.
"I believe there will be no steps take that will mean a setback for the aspiring members in the near future," Kovacs added.
